# Free subgroups generated by specified rose letters in the four-line laws

## Statement

In the four-line law and its bounded finite-color perturbations considered in [C51](Yin_C_A0051_v1.md#geometric-safeguards-under-the-change-of-counts), [L53](../ledger/Yin_L_A0053_v1.md#matching-safeguards-and-the-relative-mod-two-quotient) and [C54](Yin_C_A0054_v1.md#many-opposite-cycles-and-simultaneous-open-lifts), use the indicated fixed small logarithmic girth scale and admissible sizes for the chosen law.
Let \(S\) be an inverse-closed subalphabet of the rose letters and let \(M_S=(w(t,u))_{t,u\in S}\) be the restriction of the [source turn-weight matrix](../literature/pdf/Ope26f.pdf#page=4), including its zero entries at immediate reversals.
With probability tending to one in the girth-conditioned law, simultaneously for every such \(S\) with spectral radius \(\rho(M_S)<1\), the free group on the selected inverse pairs embeds in the original cone group \(G_n\).
There is a constant \(C_S\), independent of \(n\), such that each reduced \(S\)-word \(u\) satisfies
\[
                    |u|_S\le C_S\,|\bar u|_{G_n}
\]
in the rose word metric. Here \(\bar u\) denotes its image.

In particular all choices of at most 62 inverse pairs work.
Up to 64 pairs work whenever at most two of them are the mixed extra–ordinary pairs.
These assertions cover arbitrarily long words on the chosen letters.
They hold together with the no-\(C_{21}\) conclusion for the [fourteen-color exceptional family](Yin_C_A0054_v1.md#excluding-all-orders-with-prescribed-simple-composition-factors) when its finite list includes \(C_3\).
The probabilistic claims use a strengthened bounded-pattern event proved below, not just a deterministic girth condition.
The last section also gives the corresponding test for the readable words of a finite immersed graph fixed before sampling.

## Bounded path systems with some comparisons replaced by an alphabet restriction

Fix \(S\) as in the statement, discarding the empty case.
For any \(h\), sum the weight \(P(W)=\prod w(t_i,t_{i+1})\) over all words of length \(h\) on \(S\).
This sum is \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T} M_S^{h-1}\mathbf1\). Finite-dimensional matrix powers and \(\rho(M_S)<1\) bound it by \(C e^{-\xi h}\) for some \(\xi>0\).
Thus for full grid blocks of length \(s+O(1)\), the number of \(S\)-words in the bin \(d=\lfloor-\log P(W)\rfloor\) is at most \(\exp(d-\xi' s)\) for some \(\xi'>0\) and all sufficiently large \(s\).
This bound uses the first power of the word weight, while the unrestricted bin count in Ope26f (3.9) uses the square.

Use the ordinary cyclic path systems of [Ope26f, Proposition 3.1 and its proof](../literature/pdf/Ope26f.pdf#page=7), with no rooted path needed here.
Allow a bounded number of distinguished disjoint intervals of previously unpaired positions whose letters must all lie in \(S\).
Call the remaining unpaired positions unrestricted, and write \(b\) for their count.
We claim that for some \(\varepsilon>0\) chosen before the fixed path, length and interval-count bounds, the probability of such a system with \(L\le H\le C_0 L\) and \(b\le\varepsilon H\) is \(o(1)\).
Keep the usual condition that matched occurrences traverse distinct underlying edges.

To verify the modification, mark all endpoints of distinguished intervals as additional cuts in the source chain and offset construction.
The length tuples and cuts have polynomially many choices for fixed pattern bounds.
The image graph, bounded multiplicities, stage exponent \(\sum_j(V_j-E_j)\le0\), and full-block subdivision consequently satisfy the same estimates as in (3.2)–(3.6), with only boundedly many additional cuts.
Away from these cuts, an unmatched block occurrence either lies wholly in an \(S\)-interval or consists of unrestricted positions.
Call other unmatched occurrences bad along with those consisting of unrestricted positions, so that \(s\) times the number of bad occurrences is at most \(b+o(L)\).
Indeed only boundedly many block occurrences are incident to a cut or chain end, with the same rounding loss as in (3.6).
The restricted letters of a full occurrence constrain the word of its underlying block even if read backwards, since \(S=S^{-1}\).

We give the altered stage selection explicitly.
Use the notation \(m_i,d_i\) of the source for block multiplicity and bin, let \(U\) be a link component, and set \(S_U=\sum_{i\in U}m_i\) and \(z=\max_{i\in U}m_i\).
The numerical product of the embedding bounds over stages supplies \(-\sum_{i\in U}m_i d_i\) in the logarithm, by (3.10).
There are constants \(\delta_0,a_0>0\) with \(\delta_0s/2\le d_i\le a_0s\) and unrestricted bin count at most \(\exp(2d_i-\delta_0s)\).
The additive \(o(L)\) propagation and rounding errors throughout are as in (3.7) and (3.11).
A self-link already leaves only the propagation error in the word count and hence has a strictly negative contribution of order \(sS_U\).
If \(2z\le S_U\), root the link component at a minimum bin and use the source's unchanged bound \(-\delta_0 sS_U/2\).

Suppose \(2z>S_U\), and choose a block \(i_*\) of multiplicity \(z\).
If any of its unmatched occurrences lies wholly in a distinguished interval, root the word count there, using the restricted bin estimate above.
At each of the \(z\) active stages there are at most \(\exp(d_{i_*}-\xi's)\) choices of the root word, with \(\exp(o(s)|U|)\) further possibilities by spanning-tree propagation.
The roots at all these stages are active. The total remaining exponent is at most
\[
        -\xi' s z-\sum_{i\ne i_*}m_i d_i
             \le -\min(\xi',\delta_0/2)sS_U
\]
before the propagation errors.
If there is no such restricted occurrence at \(i_*\), at least \(2z-S_U\) of its occurrences are bad, since the at most \(S_U-z\) partner occurrences at other blocks can serve only once each in the absence of self-links.
Using the minimum-bin root instead, (3.11) then costs at most
\[
                  -\delta_0 s S_U/2 + a_0s\,b_U ,
\]
where \(b_U\) counts bad unmatched occurrences in this component.
This exhausts the cases without charging a long interval of restricted letters to the unrestricted budget.

Summing gives \(\log\prod_j B_j\le -\kappa H+a_0 b+o(L)\) for a fixed \(\kappa>0\).
Choose \(\varepsilon\le\min(1/4,\kappa/[4(1+a_0)])\).
The number of stages is bounded once the pattern parameters are fixed, so one expected stage count is exponentially small in \(L\).
The enlarged unlabelled patterns and bin choices cost only \(\exp(o(L))\), proving the claim by a union bound.
Under the prescribed finite-color laws the same uncolored word counts upper-bound the assignments.
Color propagation cancels the per-edge block-size factor up to a bounded factor per stage, and the bounded perturbations give \(\exp(o(L))\) errors exactly as in the [four-line stage estimate](Yin_C_A0051_v1.md#geometric-safeguards-under-the-change-of-counts).
There are only finitely many rose subalphabets, independent of \(n\), allowing simultaneous use of the resulting events.

## Capped pictures with an outer segment in the chosen letters

On the usual diameter and girth events consider a reduced capped picture with at least one inner disk and a cyclically reduced outer word split into a segment on \(S\) and a segment of \(v\) arbitrary letters.
Either segment may be empty.
Let \(H\) be total inner perimeter, so \(H\ge L\).
The [free outer disk reduction of Mghirbi and Douglas, Lemmas 4.2–4.3](../literature/pdf/MD26.pdf#page=13) gives such a picture for every nonempty cyclically reduced null word with the prescribed outer reading.
We show that \(H\le 8v/\varepsilon\) on the strengthened event.

Use their [splitting, closing and cluster extraction](../literature/pdf/MD26.pdf#page=15) on the inner boundaries, cutting the outer circle at the two segment ends for the interval count.
Choose their constants \(D_0,U,\eta,K_0\) for the preceding \(\varepsilon\).
The split inner graph boundaries give \(k'\le H/L\) pieces with original lengths between \(L\) and \(UL\) and closures of length at most \(D_0 L\).
The interval lemma on the sphere, with at most two outer pieces, represents the arcs by at most \(6(k'+2)\le18H/L\) interval pairs.
Pair intervals between remaining graph pieces as usual. Distinguish as \(S\)-intervals the graph intervals originally paired to the \(S\)-segment of the outer word.
They use only letters of \(S\), regardless of orientation.
Drop the outer disk for planar separation. Deleting at most \(\eta k'\) graph pieces leaves clusters of at most \(K_0\) pieces.
Over these clusters, retained length is at least \(15H/16\) and the number of unrestricted unpaired positions is at most \(\varepsilon H/16+v\) because these positions come from closures, deleted partners or the arbitrary segment.
These are the source's inequalities (5)–(6) with only the arbitrary segment charged to the exterior loss.
Each surviving inner comparison or distinguished \(S\)-interval charges one original interval pair, hence their total count is at most \(18H/L\).
Clusters with more than \(\varepsilon H_Z\) unrestricted positions cost at most \(H/16+v/\varepsilon\) in length, where \(H_Z\) is cluster length.
Those with more than \(288H_Z/L\) comparisons and distinguished intervals cost at most \(H/16\).
If \(v\le\varepsilon H/8\), there is therefore a remaining cluster with \(L\le H_Z\le K_0(U+D_0)L\), satisfying all the bounded-pattern requirements just excluded.
All these pattern bounds are chosen after \(\varepsilon\) and before sampling.
This proves the perimeter estimate. In particular \(v=0\) rules out every nonempty cyclically reduced null word on \(S\), and hence all nontrivial freely reduced null words on \(S\) by cyclic reduction.

For the metric assertion take a reduced \(S\)-word \(u\) and a shortest word representing its image.
Form their difference as two boundary segments, and freely and cyclically tighten.
Cancellations remove a letter from each segment while both remain, since each segment itself is reduced.
If one disappears, the desired bound follows from freeness on \(S\) or from the fact that at least as many letters of the other word were present.
Otherwise let \(u',v'\) be the remaining segments and use a reduced capped picture.
No arc pairs two occurrences on \(u'\), since taking the subdisk on the side between these occurrences that avoids the other segment would make the intervening subword trivial in \(G_n\), since its inner boundaries are graph relators and the connecting arc identifies its ends.
Freeness on \(S\) makes this impossible for a nonempty reduced intervening word, and adjacent inverse letters are excluded by reduction.
Thus every occurrence on \(u'\) is paired to either an inner letter or an occurrence on the other segment.
It follows that \(|u'|\le H+|v'|\le(1+8/\varepsilon)|v'|\).
Reinserting the canceled pairs proves the required word-metric bound with the same constant.

## Which choices of letters are covered?

Let \(r\) count ordinary–ordinary inverse pairs in \(S\) and \(e\in\{0,1,2,3\}\) the mixed pairs.
For \(e=0\) each reduced ordinary turn has weight \(1/129\), so the row sum is \((2r-1)/129<1\) for \(1\le r\le64\).
For the mixed case, group letters as ordinary with ordinary inverse, ordinary with extra inverse, and extra.
Summing the source weights over destination types gives the nonnegative matrix below at the indicated maximal \(r\)'s, where \(p=129/16513\).
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
      (2r-1)/129 & e/129 & ep\\
      2rp & ep & e-1\\
      2r/129 & (e-1)/129 & ep
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \((r,e)=(63,1),(62,2),(59,3)\), respectively, this matrix sends each of the positive vectors \((10,10,10)\), \((10000,19922,9923)\), \((1000,2962,985)\) strictly below itself in every coordinate, by direct rational substitution.
Lifting the three values to their corresponding letters proves strict spectral radius below one by the weighted maximum norm.
Fewer pairs give principal submatrices of such choices, proving the stated bounds.

On the same event, two different vertices joined in one side graph by a reduced nonempty path on one of these alphabets have different original group labels.
This rules out matching those particular endpoints by any combination of cone relations, even if the proposed proof leaves the subalphabet.
It does not show that every possible partner of a particular color-\(3\) vertex lies in such a component.
Matrices over the subgroup generated by those letters act by copies of their free-group regular convolution on right cosets, with the same kernel trace.
Thus the conclusion concerns matrices of unbounded word degree on a specified part of the rose, rather than finite-radius moment convergence alone.

## A fixed finite graph of permitted turns

More generally, fix a finite graph \(Z\) immersed in the rose before drawing the tuple.
On its directed edges set
\[
 K_{ef}=\mathbf1_{\{\operatorname{end}(e)=\operatorname{start}(f),\
                          f\ne\bar e\}}\,w(\lambda(e),\lambda(f)),
\]
where \(\lambda\) is the signed label.
If \(\rho(K)<1\), with probability tending to one no nonempty freely reduced word readable as a path in \(Z\) becomes trivial in \(G_n\).
For each readable reduced word \(u\) the same comparison \(|u|\le C_Z|\bar u|_{G_n}\) holds.
In particular the image of \(\pi_1(Z)\) for a chosen connected component embeds as a free subgroup.

Indeed the sum of word weights over distinct readable words of length \(h\) is bounded above by \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K^{h-1}\mathbf1\), since counting each path counts every readable word at least once.
The language is closed under subwords and inverse reading.
In the bounded-pattern argument require each distinguished interval to read a word in this language.
Every full block contained in a distinguished occurrence then has the same restricted bin estimate as before, and all word-count and embedding bounds remain valid.
For the disk argument cut the outer boundary at the linear start and end of the readable segment even when it occupies the entire circle.
Every retained exterior contact interval then reads a subword of that segment.
Free and cyclic reduction shorten the readable segment only by trimming its ends, and the intervening subword between two putative partners on that segment is also readable.
This proves both assertions by the same estimates with the constants of \(Z\).
The claim holds simultaneously for any preassigned finite list of such graphs.
It does not permit selecting \(Z\) from a closed walk found after sampling the matching.
